metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice exactly matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. The experimental design contains many trials where TTB and Tallying make diametrically opposite predictions (e.g., TTB strongly favors A because of the highest validity cue, whereas Tallying favors B because it has a greater number of less valid cues). By computing the TTB match rate, we expect a score close to 1.0 for simulated TTB agents, and a score well below 0.5 (often close to 0.2) for Tallying agents.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the strict preference of the Tallying heuristic. The experimental design specifically pits Tallying against Take The Best (TTB) such that on all trials where Tallying has a strict preference, TTB prefers the exact opposite option (driven by the highest-validity discriminating cue). Therefore, Tallying agents will score significantly above 0.5, while TTB agents will score significantly below 0.5.

By analyzing trials where WADD and Tallying make strictly opposing predictions (e.g., when 2 high-validity features outscore 3 low-validity features under WADD, but lose under Tallying's count), we can compute the proportion of choices that align with WADD. WADD will reliably score > 0.5 (closer to 1.0) on this metric, while Tallying will reliably score < 0.5 (closer to 0.0), producing a massive and stable gap between the two theories.

The metric targets the critical dissociation trials (Trials 1 and 3) where Tallying and WADD have completely opposite preferences. In these trials, one option is endorsed by 2 high-validity features (summing to 1.8 for WADD) and the other by 3 lower-validity features (summing to 1.65). Tallying simply counts features and strictly prefers the option with 3 features. WADD computes the weighted sum and strictly prefers the option with 2 features. By calculating the proportion of choices for the option with 3 features on these specific trials, Tallying will predict a value > 0.5 (approaching 1.0), while WADD will predict a value < 0.5 (approaching 0.0).

This metric isolates trials where the top 4 features favor one option, but the 5th feature brings the total sum to a tie. For Standard Tallying, these trials are perfect ties across all 5 features, so the model predicts guessing (choice probability exactly 0.5). For Top-N Tallying, subjects who restrict their attention to the top 4 features will strictly prefer the option favored by the top 4, ignoring the 5th feature that creates the tie. Thus, Top-N Tallying predicts a significantly higher match rate with the top-4 favored option.

This metric calculates the difference in choice rates between two specific sets of trials. In the first set (Trials 1, 4, 6, 8), the top 5 features result in a tie, but the 6th feature breaks it. Theory 1 (Tallying across all features) will show a strict preference, while Theory 2 (Top-N Tallying) will guess. In the second set (Trials 2, 3, 5, 7), the top 5 features favor one option slightly, but the 6th feature favors the other, resulting in a tie across all 6 features. Theory 1 will guess, while Theory 2 will have a strict preference. By subtracting the adherence rate of the second set from the first, Theory 1 produces a positive value, whereas Theory 2 produces a negative value, cleanly distinguishing the two theories.
